def: A pituitary gonadotropin that stimulates ovarian follicle growth in women and Sertoli cell sperm support in men.
The clear fluid made by the choroid plexus that cushions the brain and spinal cord; sampled by lumbar puncture.
A hormone from the parathyroid glands that raises serum calcium and lowers phosphate.
A herpesvirus causing congenital infection and opportunistic disease (retinitis, colitis) in immunocompromised patients; owl-eye inclusions.
A pituitary hormone that stimulates the thyroid to make and release thyroid hormone.
The cell's main energy currency, releasing energy when its terminal phosphate is hydrolyzed.
A carrier of acyl groups derived from pantothenic acid (vitamin B5), central to fatty acid metabolism and the citric acid cycle.
The main blood buffer anion, regulated by the kidneys, that neutralizes acid.
The volume of plasma filtered by the kidney glomeruli per minute, the standard measure of kidney function.
A pentameric antibody that appears first in the immune response and fixes complement strongly.
A DNA virus causing warts and cervical, anal and oropharyngeal cancers; types 16 and 18 are high risk.
A pituitary hormone that stimulates cortisol release from the adrenal cortex.
A glycoprotein on helper T cells that binds MHC class II and is the receptor for HIV.
A DNA virus that causes oral and genital herpes, encephalitis and keratitis, and lies latent in sensory ganglia.
The antibody of mucosal secretions such as saliva, tears and breast milk, secreted as a dimer.
The enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II and degrades bradykinin; blocked by ACE inhibitors.
Progressive airflow limitation from chronic bronchitis and emphysema, usually caused by smoking.

term: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
def: Excess ADH causing water retention, hyponatremia, concentrated urine and euvolemia; seen with small cell lung cancer and some drugs.
A hypothalamic peptide released in pulses that triggers LH and FSH secretion from the pituitary.
The body fluid outside cells, comprising plasma and interstitial fluid, about one third of total body water.
An autoimmune disease with antinuclear and anti-dsDNA antibodies causing rash, arthritis, nephritis and cytopenias, mostly in young women.
Antidepressants such as fluoxetine and sertraline that block the serotonin transporter; side effects include sexual dysfunction and serotonin syndrome.
A cytokine released by virus-infected cells and immune cells that induces an antiviral state; type II (gamma) activates macrophages.
Infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, forming granulomas with caseous necrosis, mainly in the lungs.
The cholesterol-rich lipoprotein that delivers cholesterol to tissues and drives atherosclerosis.
A herpesvirus that causes infectious mononucleosis and is linked to Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
Widespread clotting that consumes platelets and clotting factors, causing bleeding and microthrombi; triggered by sepsis, trauma or obstetric complications.
Acute lung injury with diffuse alveolar damage, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and severe hypoxemia.
The ECG deflection representing ventricular depolarization.
The antibody that binds mast cells and basophils and mediates type I hypersensitivity and defense against parasites.
A DNA virus that causes acute and chronic hepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma; spread by blood and body fluids.
An antibiotic that inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase, usually given with sulfamethoxazole.
A toxic nitrogenous waste of amino acid metabolism, converted to urea in the liver; rises in liver failure and causes encephalopathy.
The ECG interval from ventricular depolarization to repolarization; prolongation predisposes to torsades de pointes.
The advanced stage of HIV infection with CD4 count below 200 per microliter or an AIDS-defining illness.
A cytokine from macrophages that drives inflammation, fever and cachexia; blocked by drugs such as infliximab.
A blood clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg, risking pulmonary embolism.
Failure of the heart to pump adequately, causing fluid congestion in lungs and body.
Infection of the bladder, urethra or kidneys, most often by E. coli.
Hyperandrogenism with irregular ovulation and polycystic ovaries, usually with insulin resistance.
The product of ATP hydrolysis; it also activates platelets through the P2Y12 receptor.
The human MHC genes that present peptides to T cells; certain alleles are linked to autoimmune disease.
A blood measure of urea; raised in kidney failure, dehydration and gastrointestinal bleeding.
A sulfonamide antibiotic that inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, usually combined with trimethoprim.
A kidney hormone that stimulates red blood cell production in response to hypoxia.
A Staphylococcus aureus strain resistant to beta-lactams through altered penicillin-binding protein (mecA); treated with vancomycin.
Rapid eye movement sleep, with vivid dreams, loss of muscle tone and an active EEG.
A herpesvirus causing chickenpox and, on reactivation, shingles.
The upper right region of the abdomen, containing the liver, gallbladder and part of the colon.
The pressure of oxygen dissolved in arterial blood, normally about 80-100 mmHg.
The first enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway that makes NADPH; deficiency causes oxidative hemolysis with Heinz bodies.
Antidepressants such as amitriptyline and nortriptyline that block norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake; overdose causes arrhythmias and anticholinergic toxicity.
A fetal protein; raised in hepatocellular carcinoma, yolk sac tumors and neural tube defects, and low in Down syndrome.
A liver enzyme whose rise in serum indicates hepatocellular injury.
The genes encoding the cell-surface molecules that present antigens to T cells.
The main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain.
Reflux of stomach acid into the esophagus causing heartburn, with risk of Barrett esophagus.
The lipoprotein that carries cholesterol from tissues back to the liver; high levels are protective.
The hormonal cascade that raises blood pressure and sodium retention via angiotensin II and aldosterone.
One of the herpesviruses infecting humans, numbered HHV-1 to HHV-8.
Persistent loss of kidney function or kidney damage for over 3 months.
Noncancerous prostate enlargement in older men causing urinary hesitancy and nocturia.
Infections of the bladder, urethra or kidneys, most often by E. coli.
Streptococcus pyogenes, a beta-hemolytic bacterium causing pharyngitis, skin infection and rheumatic fever.
A congenital hole in the wall between the ventricles, the commonest congenital heart defect.
The large vein returning blood from the lower body to the right atrium.
Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, chronic relapsing intestinal inflammation.
A clotting test of the intrinsic pathway, prolonged by heparin and deficiencies of factors VIII, IX, XI and XII.
The resistance to blood flow of the systemic circulation, set mainly by arteriolar tone.
Surfactant deficiency in premature infants causing atelectasis and hyaline membranes.
Drugs such as amlodipine, verapamil and diltiazem that block L-type calcium channels, lowering vascular tone or slowing the heart.
Drugs such as losartan that block the AT1 receptor, lowering blood pressure without raising bradykinin.
An RNA virus causing chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, spread by blood.
A cytokine family; TGF-beta suppresses immune responses and drives fibrosis.
Impaired renal acid excretion or bicarbonate reabsorption causing normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.
Blood tests of liver injury and synthetic function, including AST, ALT, bilirubin, albumin and INR.
A technique that amplifies a specific DNA sequence by repeated cycles of heating, primer annealing and extension.

term: Arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide
def: The pressure of CO2 in arterial blood, normally about 35-45 mmHg; reflects ventilation.
Drugs such as omeprazole that irreversibly block the gastric H+/K+ ATPase, reducing acid secretion.
A glycoprotein on cytotoxic T cells that binds MHC class I.

term: United States Preventive Services Task Force
def: An expert panel that issues graded recommendations on screening and preventive care.
Combination drug treatment of HIV with three or more agents to suppress viral replication.
A rapid decline in kidney function, classified as prerenal, intrinsic or postrenal.
Weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared; used to classify underweight, overweight and obesity.
An enzyme in liver, heart and muscle; raised in hepatocellular injury, with AST greater than ALT in alcoholic hepatitis.
Absent T-cell function, usually with absent B-cell function, causing severe infections in infancy.
Antidepressants such as venlafaxine and duloxetine that block serotonin and norepinephrine transporters.
An enzyme in muscle and heart; raised in myocardial infarction and rhabdomyolysis.
The reduced form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, a carrier of electrons to the electron transport chain.
The body water inside cells, about two thirds of total body water.
Drugs such as ibuprofen that inhibit cyclooxygenase, reducing prostaglandin synthesis.
The rate red cells settle in a tube; a nonspecific marker of inflammation.
The nephron segment after the loop of Henle where thiazides block Na-Cl reabsorption and PTH increases calcium reabsorption.
An antithyroid drug that blocks thyroid peroxidase and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion; can cause hepatotoxicity.
The predominant hemoglobin of the fetus (alpha2gamma2) with high oxygen affinity; raised by hydroxyurea in sickle cell disease.
A recording of the brain's electrical activity from scalp electrodes.
Atherosclerotic narrowing of the coronary arteries causing angina and myocardial infarction.
A drug such as omeprazole that irreversibly blocks the gastric H+/K+ ATPase, reducing acid secretion.
A pituitary hormone that stimulates growth through IGF-1; excess causes acromegaly or gigantism.
An enzyme released with cell damage; raised in hemolysis, myocardial infarction and some tumors.
Autoimmune platelet destruction by antiplatelet antibodies, causing mucosal bleeding and petechiae.
Insulin deficiency with hyperglycemia, ketone production and anion gap metabolic acidosis, mainly in type 1 diabetes.
Failure of a fetus to reach its growth potential, usually estimated weight below the 10th percentile.
A nucleotide used for protein synthesis and as the energy source for G proteins.
A hormone released from stretched atria that promotes sodium and water excretion and vasodilation.
An enzyme in bile ducts and bone; raised in cholestasis and bone disease.
A growth factor that drives angiogenesis; targeted by bevacizumab and ranibizumab.
A liver-made lipoprotein that carries endogenous triglycerides to tissues.
A family of liver enzymes that metabolize most drugs; inducers and inhibitors cause drug interactions.
An enzyme that degrades monoamine neurotransmitters; inhibited by drugs such as phenelzine and selegiline.
Visible bulging of the neck veins from raised right atrial pressure, as in heart failure or tamponade.
The reduced form of NADP+, the reducing agent for biosynthesis and for the respiratory burst.
An enzyme that breaks down cAMP or cGMP; inhibited by sildenafil (PDE5) and theophylline.
The protonated form of ammonia, excreted in urine by the kidney as a way of eliminating acid.
HIV drugs such as zidovudine, lamivudine and tenofovir that terminate the growing viral DNA chain.
A growth hormone-induced peptide that promotes growth; IGF-1 is made by the liver.
Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing absolute insulin deficiency.
Pressure kept in the airway at the end of exhalation during ventilation to prevent alveolar collapse.
A neurodevelopmental disorder of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity, treated with stimulants.
A motor neuron of the cortex or brainstem; lesions cause spasticity, hyperreflexia and a Babinski sign.
Pooled human antibodies given intravenously for immunodeficiency and autoimmune diseases such as ITP and Kawasaki disease.
The pressure exerted by CO2 in blood or gas.
A catheter-measured pressure that estimates left atrial pressure.
A heart attack with ST-segment elevation on ECG from complete coronary occlusion.
Hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and kidney injury, classically after Shiga toxin E. coli infection.
An inhaled bronchodilator such as albuterol used for quick relief of asthma.
Immune complex kidney inflammation 1-3 weeks after group A streptococcal infection, with hematuria, hypertension and low C3.
Displacement of the femoral head at the growth plate in obese adolescents, causing hip or knee pain and a limp.
Atherosclerotic narrowing of limb arteries causing claudication.
A small device placed in the uterus for long-term contraception, copper or hormonal.
A blood test of red cells, white cells and platelets.
Autoimmune destruction of small bile ducts with anti-mitochondrial antibodies, causing cholestasis in middle-aged women.
The percentage of end-diastolic ventricular volume ejected with each beat; normally above 55%.

term: Forced expiratory volume in one second
def: The volume exhaled in the first second of a forced breath; reduced in obstructive lung disease.
A leukemia of mature B cells in older adults with smudge cells; usually CD5 and CD20 positive.
Endoscopic examination of the esophagus, stomach and duodenum.
An antidepressant such as fluoxetine or sertraline that blocks the serotonin transporter; side effects include sexual dysfunction and serotonin syndrome.
Billowing of the mitral leaflets into the left atrium in systole, causing a midsystolic click.
A B-cell surface marker targeted by rituximab.
A duodenal hormone that stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion.
A potent androgen made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase, responsible for male external genital development and prostate growth.
A growth factor released by platelets that stimulates fibroblast and smooth muscle proliferation.
The lung volume remaining after a normal exhalation, where chest wall and lung recoil balance.
Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia from ADAMTS13 deficiency, with thrombocytopenia, fever, neurologic and renal signs.
Autoantibodies against nuclear components, a screening test for lupus and other autoimmune diseases.
Rupture of the fetal membranes before labor and before 37 weeks.
Ultrasound with a probe in the vagina, giving close views of the uterus, ovaries and early pregnancy.
A vasodilating prostaglandin that keeps the ductus arteriosus open; alprostadil.
A hypothalamic hormone that stimulates ACTH release.
A leukemia with the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) and BCR-ABL, treated with imatinib.
The total volume exhaled forcibly after full inspiration; reduced in restrictive disease.
Viral infection of the nose, throat and sinuses, the common cold.
The pentose phosphate pathway, which generates NADPH and ribose.
Blockage of the small intestine, most often by adhesions, causing vomiting and distension.
The endotoxin of Gram-negative outer membranes that triggers fever and septic shock.
Very high glucose and plasma osmolality without significant ketosis, mainly in type 2 diabetes.
Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency, usually with obesity.
A tumor suppressor gene for DNA repair on chromosome 17; mutations raise breast and ovarian cancer risk.
A protease made by prostate cells, raised in prostate cancer, BPH and prostatitis.
A prostaglandin that causes fever, vasodilation, cervical ripening and gastric protection.
Glomerular disease with mesangial proliferation and basement membrane thickening, producing tram-track appearance.

term: Diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide
def: A measure of gas transfer across the alveolar-capillary membrane; reduced in emphysema and fibrosis.
Anticoagulants such as enoxaparin that mainly inhibit factor Xa and need less monitoring than unfractionated heparin.
Muscle stretch reflexes such as the knee and ankle jerks, graded 0 to 4+.
